#3281. Celsius vs. e.l.f. Beauty: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is the Better Buy for 2027?

Both of these consumer brands have taken market share from legacy rivals, but one looks easier to hold for the next decade.

Investors looking for growth often turn to the consumer sector to find brands with staying power. Comparing Celsius (CELH +1.07%) and e.l.f. Beauty (ELF +3.87%) reveals two very different paths to market dominance.

Celsius provides functional energy drinks aimed at health-conscious consumers, while e.l.f. Beauty offers prestige-quality cosmetics at mass-market prices. Both companies have disrupted their respective markets by using savvy digital marketing and strategic retail partnerships to gain significant market share from established legacy competitors.

Celsius provides functional energy drinks to a global audience, focusing on fitness-minded consumers who want sugar-free options. The company sells its products through leading retailers and e-commerce platforms like Amazon and Walmart. The energy drink portfolio, which includes brands like Alani Nu and Rockstar Energy, currently holds the number three spot in the United States energy drink market.

Celsius continues to benefit from its distribution partnership with Pepsi, which accounted for nearly half of net revenue in the most recent fiscal year. On a trailing-12-month (TTM) basis through the September quarter, revenue reached nearly $3.2 billion, representing an increase of 49% year over year.

This growth pushed net income to roughly $230 million during that period. The net margin, which represents the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses are paid, was 10%. The growth in sales and net income suggests the brand is capturing significant consumer interest among beverage stocks.

Its September 2026 balance sheet showed a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.2x, suggesting the company uses very little debt relative to its equity. The current ratio was roughly 2.0x, which indicates the company's ability to meet short-term obligations with assets that can be converted to cash within a year.

TTM free cash flow was approximately $269 million, the cash a company has left over after paying for its operating costs and equipment investments.

e.l.f. Beauty offers a multi-brand portfolio including e.l.f. Cosmetics and Naturium, focusing on high-quality beauty products at accessible prices. The company reaches customers through its own website and major retail partners such as Target, Walmart, and Amazon. By leveraging social media platforms like TikTok Shop, the business maintains high visibility among younger consumers and consistently gains shelf space in specialty retailers.

Through the September quarter, TTM revenue reached approximately $1.9 billion, representing nearly 40% year-over-year growth. The company reported net income of roughly $87 million. That left a net margin of approximately 4.5% -- an improvement over the year-ago period's 1.6% but still down from the previous margin of 12.5% in fiscal 2024 ending in March.

Its September 2026 balance sheet shows a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.7x. This ratio measures how much debt a company uses to finance its assets relative to the value of shareholder equity. Its current ratio was approximately 2.6x, indicating a strong position to cover short-term liabilities.

The company generated roughly $276 million in free cash flow during the period.

Celsius faces substantial risks from its heavy reliance on a single distribution partner for its core products. The company also faces intense competition from established players like Monster Beverage. Additionally, integrating newly acquired brands like Alani Nu poses challenges related to brand overlap and potential cultural friction. Fluctuations in the costs of aluminum cans and raw ingredients could also impact future profitability.

e.l.f. Beauty operates in a crowded market where it must compete with legacy giants like Procter & Gamble and Coty. The company is highly dependent on manufacturing in China, which makes it vulnerable to shifts in trade policy or tariffs. Furthermore, the recent acquisition of Rhode carries risks related to integrating the business and retaining key personnel.

Celsius appears to be the more attractively valued option for investors right now because it trades at lower multiples than its peer.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The Forward P/E ratio measures the current stock price relative to future earnings estimates for the next year. Meanwhile, the P/S ratio measures the market value of a company relative to its sales over the past twelve months. Both metrics suggest that investors are currently paying a higher premium for the beauty brand's growth profile than for the energy drink maker's.

It's more difficult to gauge which cosmetics brands will remain durable and popular with consumers over the next 10 years. In contrast, beverage consumption among leading brands tends to be more predictable and stable over time. This is why I would rather buy Celsius, especially given that the stock is trading well off its previous highs.

Celsius shares are down about 28% over the past year and trading at about 23 times forward earnings estimates. This is attractive as its energy drink portfolio continues to hold a top market share spot among leading competitors. A stronger pipeline of new products releasing in 2027 provides a growth catalyst that could drive solid revenue and earnings growth.

Long term, analysts expect earnings to grow at an annualized rate of about 16%, which could support market-beating returns.

#3280. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3279. SoftBank faces questions on AI strategy ahead of earnings after selloff

Its shares fell 11% on Friday, days after China blocked its $5.4bn deal for ABB’s robotics business.

SoftBank Group will report quarterly results on Tuesday, as investors look for signs that its AI strategy is still on track. A sharp fall in AI stocks and a blocked robotics deal have added to the pressure, Reuters reported.

SoftBank shares fell more than 11% in Tokyo on Friday. On the same day, the cost of insuring its debt against default rose to its highest in four years.

That cost is measured by credit default swaps, which pay out if a borrower fails to repay. SoftBank’s five-year spread rose to 466 basis points, the widest since October 2022, according to Markit data cited by Reuters. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point.

The Japanese group has invested across AI model makers, data centres, chips and robotics. Its biggest bet is OpenAI. In October, SoftBank completed a $30bn follow-on investment in the ChatGPT maker, taking its stake to about 13%.

However, its robotics plans took a hit last week. China blocked SoftBank’s planned $5.4bn purchase of ABB’s robotics division, ABB said on Thursday. The Financial Times first reported the decision.

SoftBank agreed to the deal in October 2025 as a key part of its push into physical AI, which uses AI to run robots and machines. Chinese officials were worried about robotics data being sent abroad to train AI models, the FT reported.

“ABB and SoftBank are in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction,” ABB said in a statement.

SoftBank is also in talks with Chinese authorities, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Meanwhile, results of this week’s US midterm elections have raised worries about slower data-centre building. Rolf Bulk, an analyst at Futurum, told Reuters that SoftBank could take a more defensive stance.

SoftBank’s results are hard to predict, because they swing with the value of its large investment portfolio.

Separately, its mobile arm SoftBank Corp reported record first-half results on Monday and raised its full-year forecast. Revenue rose 12% to ¥3.8tn, helped by growth in cloud and AI services.

SoftBank Group shares hit a record high in May. They have since fallen by almost half since early September.

#3278. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.

Both the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Fitbit Edge are designed to do more than just count your steps, calories and sleep. They can both track multiple sports, but which one comes out on top in the water? I swam 1400 metres with both devices, using my Speedo smart goggles as the control — read on to find out more.

Before we dive into the data, check out our Apple Watch Series 12 review and Fitbit Edge review on Tom’s Guide here.

Let’s start with how these trackers measure your swimming workouts. Both use an internal accelerometer and gyroscope to recognise arm pulls and calculate how many strokes you take per length, as well as your stroke rate (strokes per minute). That said, there is a slight difference between the two trackers.

Before starting a swim workout, the Apple Watch Series 12 asks you to confirm the length of the pool you’re swimming in. This means during the workout, you’re able to see at a glance how many lengths you’ve swum. The Fitbit Edge doesn’t have a similar feature. When you get out of the pool, the Apple Watch will also give you a breakdown of how far you swam in each stroke, whereas the Fitbit Edge doesn’t.

As a control, I used my Speedo iQ Vanisher 3.0 goggles. These smart goggles give you a wealth of data when you’re back on dry land. As well as your pace, distance, and how long you spent resting at the side of the pool, you’ll also be able to see your head position, breath time and distance per stroke for each stroke.

Here’s what the Apple Watch Series 12 and Fitbit Edge recorded:

As you can see from the data, the Apple Watch Series 12 was pretty perfect in the pool, measuring exactly what my goggles did. While the goggles don’t record heart rate, according to my Oura Ring 5, my average over the course of the swim was 129 beats per minute.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Fitbit Edge, on the other hand, recorded a longer swim, and therefore a few more lengths. It would be nice to see stroke data on the fitness tracker, but again, I’d argue that the Edge is designed for the casual swimmer, not someone looking for a wealth of data.

Either way, I was impressed with the accuracy of the Apple Watch in the water. Being able to input the length of the pool and see at a glance how many lengths I’d covered allowed me to listen to my podcast (the Shokz OpenSwim Pro headphones are still my go-to) without having to keep count. During most swim workouts, I typically switch strokes every 10 lengths, so it’s a good addition to have.

I’ll be continuing to test wearables in the pool, but which of these devices would you be more interested in? Let us know in the poll below.

#3276. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3275. Tilray Raises Its Guidance for the Year. Is the Stock Finally Headed on the Right Track?

The company is consolidating Canadian operations in a move that will lead to annual cost savings of around $10 million.

Tilray Brands (TLRY -1.71%) needs to show investors that it's heading in the right direction, because for many years, it hasn't been. The cannabis stock has declined more than 97% in five years, occasionally luring in investors with growth opportunities -- often tied to a U.S. marijuana market that remains off-limits for the Canadian-based producer -- only to inevitably disappoint them later on.

Recently, the company announced a consolidation of its Canadian operations, which would enable it to generate cost savings. Thus, the company has raised its guidance for adjusted earnings for the current fiscal year. It's a welcome sign of progress for the business, but is it enough to make Tilray's stock worth buying? Let's find out.

Last week, Tilray announced that it would be consolidating operations in Canada, moving cultivation and pre-roll production from its Foss facility (based in Fenwick, Ontario) to other locations in Ontario and Quebec. While it's not a massive move, the company expects to generate annualized cost savings of $10 million. CEO Irwin Simon says these actions are due to Tilray's "commitment to operating with greater efficiency, financial discipline and a clear focus on profitability."

For its current fiscal year, which ends in May, Tilray is now projecting its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) to be within a range of $70 million to $75 million, up slightly from its previous guidance of $68 million to $75 million.

It's only an improvement on the lower end of its guidance, but it's still a positive sign that Tilray is making efforts to improve its financial position and strengthen its prospects for profitability in the long run.

An increase in adjusted EBITDA profitability is positive for Tilray, but that's also an adjusted profit figure. It's not a great reflection of how well the business is doing. What's still concerning is that the business continues to burn through cash from its operations, and its growth is choppy.

The Canadian cannabis market isn't all that enticing, as competition is high and margins are low. Meanwhile, loading up on beverage brands has given Tilray's sales a boost, but it hasn't made the business a much stronger investment overall.

Ultimately, this remains a high-risk investment, and investors are likely better off taking a wait-and-see approach. Tilray needs to do a whole lot more than just consolidate operations and raise the bottom end of its guidance to convince the market it's safe to buy the cannabis stock again.

David Jagielski, CPA has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool recommends Tilray Brands. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3273. Gal Shafir on why the SOC of 2030 will run like a software team

The SecOps stack is breaking into specialized pieces. Fig's Co-Founder and CEO argues the only way to run it at scale is the way DevOps runs cloud infrastructure: as code.

Gal Shafir, co-founder and CEO of Fig Security.

For two decades, the SIEM was the Security Operations Center (SOC). One platform ingested the data, parsed it, stored it, normalized it, enriched it, ran the detections and supported the investigations. If you had a SIEM, you had a SOC.

That model is coming apart. Gal Shafir, Co-Founder and CEO of Fig Security, spent years on the SIEM side at Google SecOps. Today he sees most large security teams already taking it apart.

“The SIEM-centric era is ending,” says Shafir. “Teams are splitting the stack into pieces that each do one thing well. Pipelines handle ingestion and filtering. One SIEM brings free ingest and great content for certain logs, another runs the custom, high-stakes detections. A data lake or object storage sits beside them for retention and hunting, with federated detection engines running across all of it. The SIEM is still there, as one first-class component. It’s just not the whole SOC anymore.”

The upside is real. Each component does its job more efficiently, data lands where it is cheapest to keep, and teams stop paying premium prices to process everything in one place.

Shafir compares it to what happened to application infrastructure.

“Apps went from client-server to Kubernetes and microservices. Everything got more scalable, more efficient and cheaper. It also got far more fragmented, and that created a whole new discipline to run it. DevOps engineers made it work because they got the tools: CI/CD, infrastructure as code, observability. SecOps is going through the same unbundling right now, without those tools.”

Every new component adds configurations, schemas and dependencies that change on their own schedule. A single detection now depends on a source, a pipeline, a parser, a schema, a field mapping and a rule, often owned by different teams in different products. Each product describes only its own corner. None of them shows the whole flow.

AI raises the stakes. Agents are arriving across the stack: analyst agents on the SIEM, hunting agents on the data lake, red team agents probing telemetry and pipelines. They all run on that same fragmented data foundation. The 2026 SANS SOC Report found that 79% of SOCs use AI or machine learning tools, but only 36% have built them into a defined SOC workflow.

“AI never doubts its input,” Shafir says. “You can have the best agents in the world, and they’ll tell you everything is fine, because the alert they should be investigating never fired. A field got renamed upstream, the rule is looking for something that doesn’t exist in the data anymore, and nobody knows.”

The people are changing as fast as the stack. AI is taking on more of the triage and investigation work that used to define the SOC. Organizations are not turning analysts into engineers to fill the gap. They are moving away from staffing analyst work that AI can now do, and hiring engineers to produce more detection and response from an infrastructure that keeps getting more complex.

Most teams are early in that shift. SOC-CMM’s SOC Maturity Report 2026, a benchmark of roughly 200 SOCs, found that “most SOCs still operate with more analysts than engineers.” The same report expects that to change: “With SOCs moving towards a higher level of automation, with and without AI, engineering will play a more important role in future SOCs.”

“Everyone we talk to is hiring engineers right now,” says Shafir. “Pipeline engineers, detection engineers, SIEM engineers. They all run one flow that has to produce detection and response, and that flow gets harder to engineer every quarter.”

Shafir points to four pressures that make the engineering job bigger every year:

“Teams are stuck between two bad options,” Shafir says. “Move slowly so nothing breaks, or move fast and risk gaps nobody finds until an incident. Neither one keeps up with the rate of change.”

Shafir’s answer is to run security operations the way DevOps runs cloud infrastructure.

Detection as Code (DaC) was the right first step, he says, but it only covers the last link in the chain.

“Putting your rules in GitHub protects the link that rarely breaks on its own. Drift happens upstream. SecOps as Code means every layer, from sources and pipelines to parsers and detections, is defined, versioned, tested, shipped and rolled back as one system. Terraform didn’t version one server. It versioned the environment.”

SecOps adds a twist software teams don’t face.

“In software, you own the inputs,” Shafir says. “In SecOps, the input is logs owned by someone else, and it can change without telling you. So testing has to mean proving a rule still fires on the data as it looks today.”

“The SOC is turning into a software team,” says Shafir. “SecOps engineers were asked to adopt the DevOps mindset without ever getting the DevOps tools. That’s the gap we have to close.”

None of this is possible without full control and visibility over every part of the stack. That is the layer Fig is building.

Fig connects to any SecOps infrastructure through a read-only API and maps every data, detection and response flow, from each source through pipelines and parsers to the rules and workflows that depend on it, across every SIEM, pipeline and data lake. The mapping is deterministic, with no AI involved, so the map is ground truth. Engineers build on top of it. They design changes with the full context of their own environment, test every change before production through CI/CD with version control and rollback, and keep verifying that what shipped yesterday still works today. The same map gives AI the accurate picture of the environment it needs to be trusted.

“We don’t care whose logo is on the box,” Shafir says. “Build it or buy it, swap it next year, it doesn’t matter. Engineers should have one place to control the entire stack. Their job is to engineer security outcomes, not to manually change configurations in a dozen tools from a dozen vendors. That’s what we mean by being the operating system for SecOps.”

The SOC of 2030 won’t have fewer components. It will have more: more pipelines, more storage tiers, more detection engines, and agents built or bought for nearly every layer. What won’t change, Shafir says, is that a human engineer runs the whole stack.

The job itself will move up a level. Teams will set goals for coverage, cost and response, and systems will propose the changes to get there, such as data rerouted to cheaper storage or new detections built on data the team already collects, each one already tested. Engineers review and approve, and every change, from a person or an agent, goes through the same checks.

“Engineers should be doing security, not the bits and bytes of making the infrastructure work,” says Shafir. “The SOCs that win in 2030 won’t be the ones with the most tools or the most agents. They’ll be the ones that run their stack like software, and can change it as fast as the business and the threats do.”

Source: SOC-CMM®, SOC Maturity Report 2026 (May 2026), licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

​Over the past year, I’ve tested dozens of Bluetooth trackers, from household names like the AirTag 2 to specialized safety devices like the Pebblebee Halo. While wallet-sized tracking cards are convenient, most suffer from the same fatal flaw: they look like trackers that easily distinguish themselves over other cards you might carry.

​Anyone digging through a stolen wallet can spot an odd plastic slab immediately and toss it. However, the Statik SmartCard Incognito solves this by hiding in plain sight with a realistic credit card design. And now, it's found a permanent spot whenever I switch to a standard MagSafe wallet without support for Apple's Find My service.

With a design that lets it hide in plain sight, disguised as an ordinary credit card, the Statik SmartCard Incognito could dupe thieves to believe it's like any other card in your wallet. Powered by an rechargeable battery rated for 11 months with universal Qi wireless charging and seamless support for both Apple Find My and Google Find Hub, it's a Bluetooth tracking card that delivers total peace of mind.

​Most tracking cards are dead giveaways in a wallet. Between their extra bulk and distinct matte or glossy finishes, they rarely look like payment cards. Models I’ve tested previously, like the original Nomad Tracking Card and the Rolling Square AirCard Pro, practically scream "Bluetooth tracker."

​The closest any device came to flying under the radar was the Nomad Tracking Card Pro, which swapped the transparent circuit-board aesthetic for clean, uniform aluminum. But the Statik SmartCard Incognito takes disguise a step further by ditching the gadget look entirely in favor of an authentic credit card disguise.

​With a faux magnetic stripe on the back, a simulated chip on the front, and realistic details down to an expiration date, it blends effortlessly into a stack of plastic. Better yet, at just 1.8 mm thick, it easily undercuts the Nomad Tracking Card Pro’s bulkier 2.5 mm frame.

​While I appreciate the clever design, what matters most is actually being able to track it down. Luckily, the Statik SmartCard Incognito checks off all the boxes and delivers everything I could ask for in an everyday wallet tracker.

​One of its best perks is dual compatibility: it supports both Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub network, whereas many competing trackers require buying separate models for each ecosystem. That means I can pair it with either an iPhone or an Android device, making it an effortless stocking stuffer for just about anyone since it’s platform-agnostic.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

​Just like standard tracking cards, I can pinpoint its location through the Find My app on my iPhone — complete with a map overview, battery status, and the option to display contact details if it's placed in Lost Mode. I can also share the tracker with family members, which is especially handy for shared items like travel pouches or key wallets.

​If I misplace my wallet nearby, I can ping the SmartCard Incognito to play a loud chime through its built-in speaker. I can’t tell you how many times that simple alert has saved me when rushing out the door for my morning commute.

​While plenty of ultra-slim trackers still force you to keep track of finicky proprietary dongles, the Statik SmartCard Incognito embraces universal wireless charging.

​Statik managed to squeeze a 150 mAh rechargeable cell into its razor-thin frame, delivering up to 11 months of tracking per charge. Instead of hunting down replacement coin-cell batteries like you have to with an AirTag, you just drop this onto any Qi charging pad or flat MagSafe stand for a quick recharge. There are no bespoke cables to lose, making the maintenance virtually frictionless.

​At $29, the SmartCard Incognito sits right in line with the competition —except here, you get a tracker that actively hides in plain sight. That realistic credit card facade gives you vital extra time to track your wallet down before anyone realizes there's a beacon inside. If you want reliable tracking without advertising to the world that your wallet is tagged, this is about as seamless as it gets.

#3271. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3270. The AI Trade Is Splitting in 2: Here Are the Winners and Losers

One of the biggest bottlenecks in artificial intelligence is creating a group of haves and have-nots.

Artificial intelligence has been the driving force behind the current bull market, but some cracks are starting to appear in the megatrend. The entire industry has been under pressure over the last month, and there's a growing divide in outlooks across various segments of the AI market. That divide could grow wider over the next few quarters, creating clear winners and losers.

The days when any company related to artificial intelligence could find success in the stock market may be coming to an end. Here's what investors need to know.

Perhaps the biggest bottleneck for most companies building new data centers is access to capital.

Alphabet (GOOG +3.15%) (GOOGL +3.47%), Amazon, and Microsoft have funded much of their build-out using free cash flow from their massive businesses outside of cloud computing. All three, however, have recently been pushed to raise more outside capital to fund their build-outs, with Alphabet and Amazon producing negative free cash flow in recent quarters.

The neocloud companies that stand up data centers more quickly and offer simple infrastructure as a service are almost fully reliant on debt. CoreWeave (CRWV +4.93%) may be the worst of the bunch. It held $51.4 billion in debt and lease liabilities on its balance sheet, as of the end of the second quarter, with just $6.4 billion in cash.

Rising interest rates and declining confidence in the returns for AI spending have led to a rising cost of capital for everyone in the industry. S&P Global recently revised Meta Platforms' outlook to "negative" from "stable" due to the uncertainty around its AI spending. That's pushed the spread it pays above the risk-free rate on new debt significantly higher.

But the rise in Meta's debt pricing isn't nearly as much as the neoclouds. Oracle, for example, has seen its spread widen from less than 200 basis points to 275 basis points over the last two months. Yields on CoreWeave's debt have topped 15% recently, and it, along with other neocloud companies like Nebius, have been effectively shut out of the bond market, according to a report from the Wall Street Journal.

While the hyperscalers might have to pay a little bit more for access to capital, at least they have access to one of the most important resources for their continued growth.

Voters elected Democrat governors and representative majorities in several key states, which could result in policies that grow the divide between hyperscalers and neoclouds. Democrats had a surprising victory in Texas, which could have governor-elect Gina Hinojosa extend the temporary moratorium on data centers imposed by outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott.

Texas is the state with the most planned data center construction. Democrats also now control the executive branch in the three states that follow Texas: Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona. UBS analysts estimate about 30% of expected 2028 capacity additions are at risk of delays following the election.

That increases the value of existing data centers and projects already cleared and funded, such as those owned by the hyperscalers. Meanwhile, the neoclouds, which typically build faster, could see significant delays in expanding capacity while their debt loads continue to weigh on earnings. That will grow the divide between the two groups.

It's worth noting that neoclouds aren't the only companies that stand to lose. Chipmakers like Nvidia (NVDA -3.82%) will also see a negative impact if neoclouds aren't able to build as quickly as planned. That's especially true considering neoclouds typically stick with Nvidia chips for most of their servers. Meanwhile, the hyperscalers use custom silicon chips for a growing share of their servers due to the capital efficiency and performance they provide for their own AI development and their customers. That's been reflected in the sell-off in semiconductor stocks over the past month or so.

Investors looking to maintain a position in AI stocks should consider reducing exposure to neocloud companies and GPU makers while maintaining exposure to the hyperscalers. In fact, the recent sell-off across tech stocks may be presenting buying opportunities among hyperscalers right now.

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

#3268. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3267. Tesla to refund many Cybertruck deposits before production ends, Musk says

Orders far outpace what the Texas factory can build before the Cybertruck line shuts in about eight months, Musk said.

Elon Musk at VivaTech in Paris, 16 June 2023

Tesla will have to refund deposits to many Cybertruck customers because orders far exceed what it can build, chief executive Elon Musk said on Monday, in a post on X.

The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.

This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.

“We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people,” Musk wrote.

He did not say how many customers would get refunds, or how much money was involved.

The post follows Musk’s announcement on Friday that Tesla will start winding down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027. The move will free up space to build more Cybercabs, Tesla’s robotaxi.

Musk has also said Tesla will add an extra production shift to fill outstanding Cybertruck orders before the line is taken apart, Reuters reported.

The factory near Austin is the only known Tesla plant that builds the pickup. It is not clear whether the truck will be made anywhere else.

The Cybercab is a two-seat car with no steering wheel or pedals, and the company began building it in Texas earlier this year and started offering paid rides in Austin in September.

Tesla unveiled the steel-bodied Cybertruck in 2019 and began deliveries in late 2023, after several delays. Musk once said the truck could sell 250,000 units a year.

Tesla raised Cybertruck prices again in August, putting the cheapest version at $74,990. Last month it also cancelled reservations in Australia and New Zealand, nearly seven years after it began taking them, according to Not a Tesla App.

Sales have fallen far short of that. US sales fell 48% to 20,237 last year, down from 38,965 in 2024, according to Kelley Blue Book. Sales in the first nine months of this year fell a further 28%, the Associated Press reported, citing the same data.

In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made” and the wind-down the “end of an era”.

The Cybercab plays a central role in Musk’s plan to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company. Tesla lists an installed capacity of more than 125,000 Cybercabs a year at the Texas plant.

#3265. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

#3264. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Hybrid demand, not battery electric, is the base Toyota is building on, a sequencing choice that shapes how much its growth depends on EV adoption.

On its second-quarter fiscal year 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Toyota (TM +1.08%) raised its full-year operating income forecast by JPY 500 billion to JPY 3.9 trillion. Expanding high-margin value-chain services and sustained demand for hybrid vehicles are fortifying cash flow.

Three key takeaways from management highlight how the automaker plans to sustain this momentum.

Toyota is turning its internal factory automation needs into an external commercial growth driver. By automating plants and standardizing manufacturing skills, the company plans to sell robotics systems across supply chains and new industries.

Mass-market electrification strategy centers on high-margin hybrid sales to generate steady capital. Management is building its battery-electric business directly on top of a 10-million-vehicle hybrid foundation, aligned with real customer adoption rates.

With 150 million vehicles operating globally, Toyota is leveraging maintenance, replacement parts, and financial services to build recurring revenue streams. Higher customer retention rates and longer ownership cycles are designed to insulate earnings from cyclical downturns in vehicle sales.

Consolidated profitability is rebounding as management disciplines pricing and expands value chain earnings across key regions. Management is actively optimizing capital allocation while shrinking treasury stock holdings.

Robust structural advantages in production efficiency and global supply distribution continue to support long-term capital strategy. Executive leadership remains focused on balancing strategic investments with growing cash returns to shareholders.

#3262. EU sues IBM, Atos and Leonardo over border system delays, FT reports

EU agency eu-LISA is taking the three firms to court over late delivery of its Entry/Exit System for travellers.

The European Union has sued IBM, French IT group Atos and Italian defence company Leonardo over years of delays in developing its new biometric border system, the Financial Times reported on Monday.

The case was brought by eu-LISA, the EU agency responsible for large-scale IT systems used in border management and security. According to its annual accounts, published in July, the agency filed the lawsuit in Estonia in December 2025, where it is based.

A spokesperson for Harju County Court, Estonia’s largest district court, confirmed to the FT that the civil case had been filed there.

No hearings have yet taken place or been scheduled.

The dispute concerns the Entry/Exit System (EES), which records the fingerprints and photographs of non-EU travellers when they first enter the Schengen area, covering 29 countries. The system is designed to identify people who overstay their permitted time or are wanted by authorities.

Originally scheduled to launch in 2022, the EES only became fully operational in April this year. Its rollout was also plagued by technical problems, with faulty fingerprint scanners contributing to long queues at European airports over the summer.

eu-LISA told the FT that the legal dispute had “no impact on the functioning of the Entry/Exit System (EES), which is fully operational across Europe”. The European Commission said the case concerned delays during the system’s development, rather than its current operation.

In 2019, eu-LISA awarded the three companies a €142m contract to build the system’s core infrastructure, according to earlier reports. The contract’s value increased to €212m in 2021, the FT reported.

Correspondence seen by the newspaper shows that the agency and the contractors had been arguing over missed deadlines and financial penalties for several years. In October 2021, Atos Belgium and IBM Belgium challenged a fine, citing external factors including the Covid-19 pandemic. In February 2022, all three companies objected to revised deadlines and criticised the agency’s management.

The contract expired last year, and a new group of companies has since taken over the work. However, eu-LISA said Atos, Leonardo and IBM remained responsible for the project until August.

A 2024 Bloomberg investigation found that agency documents attributed much of the delay to Atos. The FT subsequently reported that the company had used its Moscow office to purchase software for the system. eu-LISA said it had found no security breaches.

Leonardo and Atos declined to comment to the FT, and IBM did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment.
