AI’s water problem goes beyond your chatbot — here’s what a new study found

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI has become integrated into our lives whether we like it or not. Despite big tech forcing schools to choose and lawsuits highlighting its dangers, the controversial technology is here to stay.New research published in Environmental Science & Technology puts specific AI concerns on a global map, highlighting 9,347 identified data centers, with roughly a quarter located in areas where water demand would exceed available supply for at least one month a year.

Data centers use water to remove heat from their equipment. In evaporative cooling systems, some of that water evaporates rather than returning to the local water system. Electricity generation and hardware manufacturing add an indirect water footprint, too, according to the Pacific Institute.

Where and when that consumption happens matters. The institute warns that data center water demand peaks during hot, dry periods, when supplies may be constrained, and other users also need more. Meeting those peaks can require additional utility infrastructure and spending.

“They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms,” study lead author Lorenzo Rosa said in an American Chemical Society release.

That makes data center construction relevant to people who may never pay for an AI subscription. Before approving a facility, a community needs to understand whether its water system can accommodate a large new customer during a dry summer.

Cities and municipalities are the largest water users, accounting for nearly 41% of the facilities studied, while agriculture is the primary user, accounting for another 28%, according to the American Chemical Society.

The Potomac River basin offers a useful example. An analysis by the Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin describes current average data center water consumption in the Washington metropolitan area as relatively small. Its estimated 2025 average was about 4 million gallons a day, with peak-day consumption of approximately 15 million gallons.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Cooling choices help explain the variation. Around 40% of facilities in the analysis rely exclusively on air cooling, while many others take advantage of cooler winter weather to reduce cooling demands. The commission cautions that approaches using less water often require more energy.

For residents, an annual consumption figure only answers part of the question. They also need to know how much water a facility could require during the hottest days, when local supplies may already be under pressure.

The same global study also examined existing data center locations under a scenario of 3°C of global warming relative to around 1900. The share exposed to water shortages rose to roughly a third. That projection applies future climate conditions to the facilities identified in the study; it doesn’t account for where additional data centers might be built.

Better disclosure would make proposed projects easier to assess. The Pacific Institute identifies a lack of standardized reporting on data center size, location and water use as an obstacle for communities and water managers.

Residents deserve clear answers about a proposed facility’s water source, expected summer demand and plans for drought. They also deserve to know who would pay for any necessary infrastructure upgrades.

If a data center is proposed near your home, get answers now. Start with your local planning board or water utility and ask where its cooling water would come from, how much it could use on the hottest days, and what would happen during a drought.

Be direct and ask who would pay for any water-system upgrades, too, and whether the operator would be required to make its water use public. Those details can help residents assess a project before approval.

To learn more about the infrastructure behind AI, start with Google’s data center water reporting or Microsoft’s local environmental fact sheets. These disclosures can help you understand water use where facilities operate, though they won’t tell you the footprint of your individual chats.

#3259. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3258. Nasdaq Stock Market Correction: 3 AI Stocks You Can Buy Right Now and Hold Forever

Thursday's sell-off hit the AI chip stocks with strong businesses hard. That could be an opportunity for long-term investors.

When most investors think about a stock market correction, they think about fear, and this past Thursday had plenty of it. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Nov. 5, leaving it 12% below its Oct. 6 record close and officially in correction territory.

Chip stocks took the worst of it. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 12% in a single day, on fears that the new Democratic majority in Congress will slow the build-out of AI data centers.

Let’s be clear. Although it’s certainly not fun to watch the value of your investments plunge, corrections like this are a normal part of investing, even if they never feel that way. And it’s important to emphasize that nothing has actually changed about AI demand, and no new rules have been enacted. That's why I think the sell-off created a buying opportunity in three of the most notable AI leaders.

Nvidia (NVDA -4.32%) is an AI stock that needs no introduction, but it hasn't been this cheap in a while. In its most recent quarter, revenue more than doubled, up 106% year over year to more than $96 billion, and data center revenue grew 117% to $89 billion. Management guided for about $108 billion in revenue for the current quarter, and that forecast assumes no data center revenue from China. Gross margin was 75%, which shows Nvidia still has enormous pricing power.

Even so, the stock closed at $181.60 on Thursday, 24% below its October record, and trades for less than 16 times forward earnings. Nvidia is also putting its cash to work, with a $235 billion total buyback authorization following a $150 billion increase in September. The next big test comes on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports its third-quarter results, but this could be an opportunity to add the chipmaking leader to your portfolio at a discount.

Broadcom (AVGO +7.43%) designs custom AI chips for some of the world's largest tech companies, as well as the networking gear that connects them. Its AI semiconductor revenue soared 221% year over year to $16.7 billion last quarter, and management expects that number to reach $21.7 billion this quarter. CEO Hock Tan said demand for custom AI accelerators and networking "continues to be very strong."

Despite that, Broadcom fell more than 10% on Thursday and is roughly 40% below its June record close. At about 17 times forward earnings, with $13.7 billion in quarterly free cash flow and a growing dividend, it's one of the more reasonably priced ways to own AI infrastructure. Total revenue is expected to grow 93% this quarter to about $34.8 billion, which is incredible growth, especially for a company of Broadcom's size.

AMD’s (AMD +9.43%) drop during the market sell-off was especially hard to watch. Just two days earlier, AMD reported 45% revenue growth, guided well above expectations for the fourth quarter, and said it expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. The stock still fell 17% on Thursday and is now more than 30% below its record close, even after a significant rebound on Friday.

In other words, the business looks stronger than ever, and the stock is much more attractive than it was a month ago. Unlike the other two, AMD isn’t a cheap stock, still trading at about 37 times forward earnings, but it also has a larger market opportunity ahead, so its growth rate could be sustainable for years to come.

To be sure, if the sell-off's premise proves correct and data center construction slows meaningfully, all three companies would feel it. Volatility is also likely to stay high, especially heading into Nvidia's report. But I'd rather buy great businesses (which will still be great businesses, even if the data center boom slows) after a policy scare than after a run to all-time highs.

Having said all that, corrections are a normal part of investing, and they often create the best opportunities to buy great companies. Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD all just showed that AI demand is still accelerating. For long-term investors, Thursday's sell-off looks more like an opportunity than a warning.

#3256. Meta’s Dave Wehner leaves to become CFO of AI start-up Fireworks

Dave Wehner will run the AI inference start-up’s finances as it prepares a new round. Reports put its next valuation at $30bn or more, against $17.5bn in July.

Dave Wehner has spent 14 years at Meta, more than eight of them as chief financial officer. On Friday, he announced that he is leaving his role as chief strategy officer to become CFO of Fireworks, an AI inference start-up.

The Information first reported the move on Friday evening. Wehner joined Facebook in 2012 as vice president of corporate finance and business planning. He became CFO in 2014 and moved to the strategy role in 2022.

“Fireworks has the right mission for the moment,” Wehner wrote on X.

In the post, he thanked Mark Zuckerberg and said he was “incredibly optimistic” about Meta’s future. He said he had known Fireworks chief executive Lin Qiao for a long time and wanted to join a founder-led growth company.

“I see AI as the most consequential technology shift of my lifetime. I’m excited to get to work and help build a business at the center of it,” he wrote.

Lin told CNBC that Wehner will scale the company’s finances and operations. She also wrote about the hire on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again,” Lin wrote.

Meta chief operating officer Javier Olivan also gave CNBC a statement.

“Dave helped guide Meta through tremendous growth and complexity over 14 years, and brought disciplined thinking to some of our hardest company-level decisions,” Olivan said.

Former Meta and Google employees founded Fireworks in 2022. Its platform lets developers customise and run open AI models for their businesses. It raised $1.5bn in July at a $17.5bn valuation, in a round led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV. Nvidia and Sequoia Capital are also backers.

Two outlets have reported on its next round. Business Insider reported in October that it was in early talks to raise at a valuation of $30bn to $40bn. The Information now reports that Fireworks will start a new round next week, citing people familiar with the matter. It is targeting a valuation of at least $30bn, The Information reported. TNW has not independently verified either report.

Other inference start-ups have also raised big rounds in recent weeks, including Fal at $16bn and Baseten’s planned round.

Before Facebook, Wehner was CFO of Zynga and a managing director at the investment bank Allen & Co., The Information reported. He also sits on the board of Aurora Innovation, which makes self-driving technology for trucks.

A low-cost way to start seeds in the colder months

With cold temperatures and frosty soil, winter is hard enough for your existing garden let alone trying to plant any new seeds. And, if like me, you're lacking indoor space and don't have an external greenhouse then this hack might be the game changer you're looking for.

I've been researching about setting up my own mini greenhouses while I wait to plant these 7 winter-hardy vegetables in February. While there were several ideas on what to buy, I stumbled across a TikTok that said I could make them pretty easily yourself – and all I'd need is a milk jug. So, I thought I'd give it a try. Here's what happened.

Sharing DIY home and garden tips on TikTok, @sandra.maria.home has almost 65k followers watching her videos, but it was what she had to say about milk jugs that really caught my attention.

In one video, she explains: "This is a milk jug greenhouse method I have perfected over the years. A mini greenhouse lets you start seeds outdoors way earlier without grow lights or without bathing seedlings inside. For me, it's the start of the growing season."

And all you need is a milk jug (or several, depending on how many seed starters you're planning), a pair of scissors, a kitchen knife and some duct tape. And, of course, some soil and your seeds.

Sandra has some advise from her years of mini greenhouse making when it comes to the soil you choose: "Don't use anything with fertilizer, it's too harsh for the seedlings and will kill them."

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

And, if you're planning on planting multiple seeds, use a pen or wax pencil to number the jugs so you don't lose track of which ones are which. Once spring comes around, you can gently release the duct tape and let the plants acclimatize for planting in your yard.

If you haven't already got duct tape lying around the house, you can pick it up for just under $4 to secure the edges of your mini greenhouse. It's durable, heavy duty and has excellent adhesion. If your duct tape is struggling to stick in the cold, Sandra recommends heating it up with a hair dryer.

While Sandra says she picks her jugs up at her local coffee shop, which is a seriously clever idea, I live in a busy household where we happen to drink a lot of milk. Or, at least enough for me to collect a few jugs myself.

So, milk jugs in hand, I followed her steps using scissors to cut and make drainage holes as I found this a lot easier. I then lined them up in my yard in a place I knew I could keep an eye on them without having to venture too far.

Another piece of advice that I think is worth mentioning from Sandra's video is that she says to densely pack the seeds in since this small jug of soil won't be their forever home. That means there will be more to move over once spring rolls around and they can grow into their new environment.

Sure, I need to wait and see how effective my mini greenhouses actually are when spring comes around, but I'm happy that I didn't waste any money and hardly any time doing it. So, if some seeds are successful and others aren't, I'll still be happy to try again.

What I loved about this gardening hack is that making the mini greenhouses really took me no time at all – and it also didn't cost me anything. Considering how easy and affordable this hack is, I'll definitely be recommending it to friends. I just might wait until next year, so I can show them proof that it really does work. Not that I don't trust Sandra!

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

#3252. Beyond the Election: 4 ETFs I'm Continuing to Buy No Matter What the Market Does in 2027

Now could be a good time to take advantage of short-term volatility.

The Invesco QQQ ETF, which tracks the Nasdaq 100 index, is down more than 13% from its October high. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is holding up modestly better, only down about 6% from its high. Much of this decline has happened since the U.S. midterm election, where Democrats won races across the country and will be in the majority in both the House and the Senate.

This past week will test investors' stomachs and whether they view the current stretch as an opportunity to buy the dip or a reason to run for the exits. Short-term volatility can feel painful and make your brokerage account look even worse. But if you're a long-term investor, this should be viewed as a normal bump in the road that can be taken advantage of.

That's why I'd still look at buying four ETFs for 2027 and beyond.

If you're still building up the core of your portfolio or want to establish a foundational position, the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +1.86%) remains one of the best choices for U.S. equity exposure. It goes beyond just the S&P 500 to include mid-cap and small-cap stocks, two groups that have been outperforming large-caps in 2026.

In my opinion, there's never really a bad time to add the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF or the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF to your portfolio as long-term holdings. The current election volatility, however, allows you to pick up shares at a 6% discount and bump up your returns once stocks recover.

When the market begins to look uncertain, quality matters. It's the one factor that investors tend to gravitate toward in search of safety. The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD +0.65%) does it better than perhaps any other ETF. It looks at several balance sheet fundamental metrics to select quality dividend-paying stocks, helping to ensure the fund is a portfolio built to withstand a potential downturn.

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF has staged an impressive rebound in 2026 following three years of disappointing returns. It's clearly been helped by its overweight in energy stocks, but the overall diversity of sector holdings -- big overweights in consumer staples and healthcare -- helps ease tech reliance in your portfolio and add some defensive posturing should the markets continue to correct.

If you're not looking for quality within the dividend stock universe specifically, you could choose the Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF (SPHQ +2.18%) instead. It similarly examines several numbers, including return on equity (ROE), accruals, and financial leverage, to help identify quality stocks with durability and sustainability.

While quality is never a bad idea to overweight in uncertain markets, you need to be a little careful with the Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF. It still has over 30% invested in tech and has Microsoft, Apple, and Nvidia as its top holdings. But if 2027 earnings forecasts deliver as expected, tech stocks should be able to rebound from this correction. Earnings tend to be the big driver of stock returns, and I still view this as a longer-term tailwind for now.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP +1.50%), of course, is a way to invest in U.S. large-caps without the tech-heavy concentration. The S&P 500's biggest risk right now is that 40% of the index is invested in tech stocks, with a large percentage coming from just 5-10 names. This fund helps solve that problem by indirectly underweighting tech and reallocating to other areas of the market.

Like the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF is a good way to retain your focus on large-caps while diversifying your holdings. Non-tech earnings growth is finally starting to look stronger as second-level artificial intelligence (AI) build-out beneficiaries. This could end up being a smart way to play the next stage of the AI trade.

If you read any review for Apple’s new MacBook Pro, you will see a lot of folks drooling over the new PROLED XDR display. And they’re not wrong — flawless color calibration, a new touchscreen interface and up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness.

But if you look past the shiny new Dynamic Island, you’ll see a darker reality. One where what I like to call “OLED washing” is happening.

Apple didn’t build a machine for the next generation of computing (local AI). They built a $2,899 luxury item. If you want to see what a real, weaponized local AI computer looks like in 2026, you need to look away from Cupertino and start looking more closely at the better value-for-money monsters being built with Nvidia’s RTX Spark and AMD’s Strix Halo inside.

Yes, we are currently living through RAMageddon, a brutal memory shortage driven by enterprise data centers hoarding silicon. While I do see cracks in this cloud AI bubble, it’s going to be here for a while.

Apple’s response to this was to slap a near-three racks starting price on the 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro and give you a paltry 24GB of unified memory.

It’s both overkill in some ways — that tandem OLED screen might be worth it if you are a Hollywood color grader editing 8K ProRes video for example.

But in others, for those moving into the era of ditching the data center and running local agentic AI directly on our hardware — 24GB is a tough pill to swallow.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

It’s effectively a multi-million dollar mansion with only one bathroom. It looks gorgeous from the street, but the moment you invite guests over (or spin up a local 70B parameter LLM), the plumbing completely collapses.

While Apple is obsessing over making their chassis lighter and adding a touchscreen nobody asked for, the Windows ecosystem has been quietly preparing for a value war.

Just a few weeks ago, I balked at the high $5,899 price tag for the 128GB version of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra that I tested. And then, I saw the equivalently-specced 14-inch MacBook PROLED come in at $7,099 ($7,399 for the 16-inch).

And yes, the PROLED does have a much better display, better CPU performance and a longer battery life. But, are those uplifts worth an additional $1,200? I’m not sure.

Waterloo Battle Analysis prompt (Meta Llama 3.1 8B)

Plus if you are leaning more towards local AI, the tokenomics of an RTX Spark are a little better than M5 Pro too. M5 Max is faster, but you'll have to pay much more for that (as you can see).

If the tandem OLED is important, then the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ may have a terrible name, but at $6,799, it’s still $300 less.

And I haven’t even gotten to the AMD side of things yet. The Strix Halo chip has grown into quite the AI-capable silicon over its life. And that longevity means you can find some good options with more money for much less money than taking a bite of the Apple.

This is definitely one for those with more of a gaming persuasion, but it's a strong chip for local AI workloads with 8GB more memory than the MacBook Pro for much less.

If you don't want to give up the slick utilitarian aesthetic and the OLED display, the Yoga Pro 7a is the option to go for. Still more memory, and still $600 less.

Taking things to the next level is what's essentially a far superior Surface Pro with a monster amount of memory. For context, to get this amount, you'll need to spend $3,800 more for the MacBook PROLED equivalent.

So as you can see, whether you want a better balance of memory, want to keep that OLED display, or want to go all out (that Z13 with 128GB for $3,800 less is looking mighty tempting), you can get much more local AI headroom with these machines too.

So let me be clear, because I don’t want this to be me dunking on Apple here. The MacBook PROLED has easily won the display and battery life war this year — that screen is a masterclass. But the “why not” era can easily blind you from picks that offer better bang for your buck.

Apple’s charging you $3,000 for a reference monitor so you can have a prettier interface when you ask Siri to summarize your emails. Meanwhile, the RTX Spark and Strix Halo laptops give you the raw compute and massive memory pools to actually build this local agentic future on your desk.

#3249. Apple Intelligence registered in China for use on iPads and Macs

Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator approved the filing weeks before Apple’s AI service, powered by Alibaba’s Qwen, launches in China.

The Apple Store in Nanjing, China, lit up at night.

Apple’s AI service, Apple Intelligence, has been cleared for use on tablets and laptops in China. The cyberspace regulator in Shanghai made the change on Monday, Reuters reported.

The regulator said Apple’s iPads and Mac laptops had been added as two new uses in the service’s filing. It made the change under China’s rules for AI services.

In China, firms must register AI models and chatbot-style services with the state before they can offer them to the public.

Apple Intelligence first won approval for use on iPhones in China in mid-July. At the time, Alibaba said its Qwen AI model would power the service on Apple’s devices in China. Baidu is also a tech partner, Bloomberg reported.

“Qwen will be integrated into Apple Intelligence experiences within iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS for users in China,” an Alibaba spokesperson told CNBC in July.

Apple first showed Apple Intelligence in 2024 and began rolling it out in other markets later that year, with iOS 18. China has waited much longer.

Apple needs local partners in China. OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which runs some Apple Intelligence tools in other countries, is not offered there.

On 31 October, Apple said on its China news site that the first features would come with iOS 27.3. A test version for app makers went live on 4 November. The full release is due in December.

In China, Qwen will run Siri, Writing Tools, and visual intelligence, which lets users ask about what the camera sees. But Siri AI and other tools Apple showed off at its June developer event are not part of the launch.

Apple’s October news listed only iPhones. These are the iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max, the iPhone Air, the iPhone Duo, and every model from the iPhone 16 on. Siri and the phone must be set to English or Simplified Chinese.

Reuters also reported in August that Apple had built its own AI model just for China with Alibaba’s help. That was a shift from its plan to rely only on outside models in the country.

Apple did not say on Monday when the features will reach iPads and Macs in China.

#3247. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

Making sure you’re in tune with the basics behind AI

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In my line of work, as someone who’s constantly explaining what I do for a living, it can be a lot for someone to wrap their head around.

Explaining that I cover the world of AI, the abundance of chatbots & AI agents that exist and the companies & bigwigs that throw big swaths of money at the growing tech can be a lot for someone to take in. I can only imagine how much more confused they get when they look up AI as a general search term and come across a bunch of additional technical jargon that scares them away from the trending tech altogether.

I went ahead and offered up a 15-minute lesson on how to start out using ChatGPT (which helped my parents get a decent understanding of one of the most popular AI tools). Now I’m here to break down seven of the most vital terms every AI user should know.

Whether you consider yourself someone who’s just starting to give AI a chance or a power user whose base level of knowledge is already strong enough, it’s still worth learning or getting a quick refresher on the world of AI.

A Large Language Model can be broken down easily by delving into what each letter in “LLM” stands for. The “L” represents the “large” amounts of data that it's trained on, such as the words contained in books, on sites, in articles and across research papers. The second “L” pertains to the human “language” that it’s designed to understand, process and generate on its own.

And finally, the “M” represents the type of AI program that works as a “model” that interprets human patterns and relationships through words instead of just memorizing answers. For instance, an LLM taps into the patterns it’s learned during its training to properly respond to a user’s request to write a birthday message to their friend. Simply put, an LLM is the driving force behind a chatbot that helps it comprehend and generate human language.

Generative AI is a type of AI that can generate original content, such as text, images, audio, videos and computer code, based on the instruction you give it via a prompt. I’m sure you’ve come across all sorts of photos of people made to look like they exist in a neon-soaked 80s world, videos of dogs riding a skateboard like a human being and easily discernible AI-generated songs. Generative AI is used to produce those types of content as it's commanded to create something new instead of just retrieving pre-existing information.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Think of machine learning as a method in which computers are taught how to recognize patterns and make predictions based on all the data they’ve observed. Instead of having to be given specific instructions by a programmer to complete their task, computers can rely on machine learning to learn from examples to build knowledge over time.

Machine learning is comparable to the way Netflix brings up recommendations, as the streaming service analyzes what you’ve watched, what you’ve given a thumbs up to and what you've skipped to make educated decisions about what to suggest you watch next. The more information Netflix has, the stronger its recommendations will be. Machine learning is the core engine that’s crucial to the continued improvement of AI as a whole.

A neural network is a computer system that’s comparable to the human brain, as it contains layers of interconnected nodes that process information and identify patterns in the same way that neurons connect and communicate in our heads. It’s the system that helps AI recognize complicated patterns, with it being able to understand that you’re presenting it with a picture of a cat since a neural network helps it learn to recognize the patterns of that animal type.

AI is prone to making mistakes, which are defined as hallucinations. When a chatbot confidently gives you information that is clearly incorrect or entirely made up, you’ve just borne witness to your AI tool hallucinating. AI doesn’t automatically recognize whether the information it's giving you is true, which can lead it to produce made-up statistics and cite fake sources. As a tip, it’s always worth double- and even triple-checking the information AI feeds you. That rings especially true for those instances where a chatbot gives you medical, financial or legal advice.

Prompt engineering is super easy to comprehend: it’s the process of writing detailed instructions that can help a chatbot produce better results for whatever you’re requesting. Now, a prompt is simply what you write into an AI tool. Prompt engineering is what you need to master so you can properly phrase your command so that the AI tool understands exactly what you want and delivers on it.

Going from a basic prompt such as “give me dinner ideas” to a more fleshed-out one such as “Give me [number] dinner ideas that take less than [time] to prepare, cost under [cost] per meal and use ingredients I can find at [name of supermarket” highlights a stronger mastery of prompting chatbots.

I’m sure you’ve spotted instances of AI subscription plans that include a limit on how many tokens your current plan consumes.

Tokens are pretty much small chunks of text that AI models process when reading and generating language. Since chatbots don’t necessarily process an entire sentence as individual words, they break up portions of the text you put into it as tokens instead. A token can be classified as a single short word, a portion of a longer word, a punctuation mark and even a period. So a question you may type into ChatGPT will push it to break up that sentence into tokens before it processes it to generate a proper response.

Since some AI models have a limit on how much information they can process during a single conversation, tokens are brought up when looking at their subscription plans so you can understand how much they can take in before they reach their limit.

As someone who couldn’t even tell you the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent just a year ago, I’ve taken crash courses on the most important terms every type of AI user should know. I’m sure all the beginners out there won’t become pros at using ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or any other AI tools overnight. But over time, you’ll recognize its benefits while also keeping the core definitions around AI as a whole in the back of your mind.

Elton Jones covers AI for Tom’s Guide, and tests all the latest models, from ChatGPT to Gemini to Claude to see which tools perform best — and how they can improve everyday productivity.

He is also an experienced tech writer who has covered video games, mobile devices, headsets, and now artificial intelligence for over a decade. Since 2011, his work has appeared in publications including The Christian Post, Complex, TechRadar, Heavy, and ONE37pm, with a focus on clear, practical analysis.

Today, Elton focuses on making AI more accessible by breaking down complex topics into useful, easy-to-understand insights for a wide range of readers.

#3244. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

#3243. These 3 Stocks Just Fell After Strong Earnings. Here’s the One I’d Buy Right Now

Shopify, Datadog and Palantir all topped expectations. Here's why investors sold, and the one I'd buy.

A good earnings report doesn't guarantee a stock will go up, and we've seen this many times throughout this earnings season. Last week, three widely held growth companies, Shopify (SHOP +0.10%), Datadog (DDOG -0.13%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR +4.11%), reported better-than-expected results, and all three stocks fell anyway.

In each case, the selling had less to do with the quarter that just ended and more to do with valuation or forward-looking guidance. Here's a rundown of what happened with each, what I think it means for investors, and which of the three I'd be comfortable buying right now.

Shopify grew its revenue by 32% to $3.74 billion in the third quarter, increased its operating income by 66%, and generated 22% of its revenue as free cash flow. Adjusted earnings of $0.49 per share beat the $0.47 consensus. The company also spent $562 million buying back its own stock, a vote of confidence from management that the stock is attractive.

The main problem was gross merchandise volume (GMV), the total value of sales on Shopify's platform. GMV grew 29% to $119.1 billion, slightly below estimates and slower than the 32% growth Shopify reported in the second quarter. As a result, the stock fell sharply on the day of the report.

I own Shopify, and I explained why I'm not planning to sell in a separate article. In short, a small GMV miss doesn't change my view of a business growing this fast while expanding its margins.

Datadog, which sells software that helps companies monitor their cloud applications, grew revenue 35% to $1.2 billion. Adjusted earnings of $0.81 per share crushed the $0.64 consensus, and management raised its full-year revenue forecast.

Like several other AI-related stocks that recently fell after strong earnings, Datadog's main issue was guidance. Datadog expects fourth-quarter revenue of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly flat with the third quarter, which is an unusual pause for a company growing this fast. Datadog had already warned that its largest customer would use less of its services starting in the third quarter, so this could be the main reason. But even so, the stock fell more than 14% the day after the report and is now about 40% below its recent high, reached in early October.

Palantir's growth is in a league of its own among the three companies discussed here. Its revenue rose 96% to $2.31 billion, U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148%, and management raised its full-year revenue forecast to about $8.53 billion. Revenue handily beat the roughly $2.18 billion consensus, and the fourth-quarter guidance came in well above expectations.

So why did Palantir's stock slip? Investors focused on bookings, which are a good indicator of revenue beyond the fourth-quarter guidance management provided. Palantir's total contract value, a measure of new deals signed, grew just 6% from a year ago, and U.S. commercial contract value fell about 31% from the prior quarter. Management said several deals had shorter terms than usual, which lowers contract value even if annual spending doesn't change.

Palantir's stock has been pricing in a lot of future growth, to put it mildly. Even after the post-earnings decline, Palantir's valuation, at roughly 53 times trailing sales, leaves very little room for any sign of slowing.

When a stock is priced for perfection, beating estimates usually isn't enough. Investors look past the latest quarter to whatever metric best predicts what is coming next. For Shopify, that was GMV. For Datadog, it was next quarter's revenue guidance. For Palantir, it was bookings growth, or the lack thereof.

Of the three, Shopify is the one I'd be most comfortable adding to after the drop. Its miss was the smallest relative to its growth, and its valuation came down the most. The margin expansion, combined with 30%+ top-line growth, should drive excellent profitability growth for years to come.

Datadog could look like a bargain if its largest-customer drag turns out to be a one-time reset, but I'd want to see revenue growth resume first. And Palantir is the most impressive business of the group, but even after the dip, its valuation assumes years of near-flawless execution.

#3242. Apple @ Work: Mac admins are shipping AI-written code with mistakes, but fixing the problems is taking days

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

There’s no doubt that AI tools are making IT admins faster at writing code, researching issues, etc. As a Mac admin, I’ve seen slow but steady growth in how I’ve used it in my daily work across all aspects of IT. It’s not perfect, though. I’ve used it to write scripts, troubleshoot networking errors, and more. A new report from Fleet puts numbers on the problem: it’s easy to ship things, but it’s hard to undo mistakes.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For this report, Fleet surveyed more than 250 enterprise IT folks who manage Apple, all with admin access to their device management systems. The folks responding to the survey manage an average of 2,000 devices, and nearly half have 6 to 10 years of Apple admin experience.

The debate over whether IT teams should use AI day-to-day is over. They already are, and in the past 30 days, 68% of those responding reported using AI for troubleshooting or log analysis, 62% used it to write scripts, and 61% used it to author device management profiles or configurations. The log analysis is something that I use AI for often. 86% allow AI-written output into production after some form of review, and only 14% keep it out of their production environments entirely. There simply is no world where IT can operate at the speed needed without AI tools.

69% of respondents can’t roll back a bad configuration change within an hour, and 43% need more than a day. Another 26% of those responding can recover the same day, but only by doing it by hand. This is the biggest red flag of the survey, in my opinion. AI lets you ship anything fast, but AI can ship bugs just like humans can.

Here’s a real scenario that can happen: an IT admin asks an AI assistant to write a configuration profile, takes a quick pass at it, and pushes it to a few thousand Macs in seconds. If something is wrong with it (a bad network setting, a restriction that locks people out of an app they need), unwinding it could take a while.

“Mac admins are basically engineers now, whether their job description calls them that or not.”

I agree with him, and I am somewhat not happy about it. The job of an Apple admin has moved a long way from deploying Macs and iPads and managing through a device management console. Today it’s identity, security, compliance, and app lifecycle, all on top of a macOS release that forces changes every year. IT teams keep getting more and more added to them without additional resources or taking things away.

31% said keeping up with Apple’s release cadence is their single biggest IT challenge, far ahead of everything else on the survey. On the bright side, Apple’s own management architecture is moving in the right direction. 53% already have declarative device management in production.

Apple has done a lot of work here, and it’s not even Apple that is to blame for the frustration. Apple has built the platform for IT to do everything it needs to do. It’s everything else. Security is harder. AI has made it harder. It’s the expectation that IT has to own AI while owning literally everything else.

IT is using AI to help with its work because it’s the only way to survive the onslaught of the AI era. You aren’t getting more help, but you’re expected to do more without anything being taken away from you. Even systems that don’t need as much day-to-day management as they did years ago, you still have to own and secure them. Hosted email is a good example here. Yes, 365 and Workspace have made it easier to keep email running. You aren’t managing servers as you did 20 years ago, but email is still not easy. You traded server management for AI-driven phishing scams, MFA management, and more. It’s two steps forward and one back. We need a period of three steps forward and zero back to get back to where IT needs to be.

You can read Fleet’s full Apple in the enterprise report on its website.

#3241. Google reportedly adds two TPU variants for secure and long-context AI

Google’s headquarters in Mountain View, California.

Google is introducing two new versions of its in-house AI chips, known as tensor processing units (TPUs), Bloomberg News reported on Monday.

The chips are called the TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max. Amin Vahdat, Google’s chief technologist for AI infrastructure, told Bloomberg they are reworked versions of existing chips, built for workloads that customers had asked for.

The 8tx is designed for secure and confidential work used by government agencies and companies in regulated industries. It runs alongside chips from AMD as part of a partnership between the two companies, according to Bloomberg’s report.

The 8i Max, by contrast, is built for AI applications that need long context windows. That means they can take in very large amounts of text or data in a single request.

Both are based on Google’s eighth-generation chips, the TPU 8t and TPU 8i, which the company unveiled at its Cloud Next event in April. The 8t is built to train AI models, while the 8i runs them once they are trained. Google said both would be generally available later this year.

Google used to release one new AI processor every two years, according to Bloomberg. This year it launched two at once, and the new variants take the eighth-generation line to four chips. Vahdat said each one is tuned for different needs.

Google first built TPUs for its own use. They have since become one of the main alternatives to Nvidia’s graphics processors, which dominate AI computing.

Google rents out TPUs through its cloud business rather than selling them as standalone chips. Anthropic agreed last year to use up to 1 million of them.

The company is also widening its chip supply chain. It works with four design partners, including Broadcom and MediaTek, to build its TPUs.

According to Bloomberg, the new variants are meant to serve an industry that is moving towards AI agents. These are AI tools that carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. At the same time, companies face growing security risks as they put such tools to work.

#3239. Remove your personal info from the web (and stop it coming back)

It seems incredible that anyone can legally create a business which involves scraping your personal data from the web and then selling it, yet here we are. There are literally hundreds of data brokers doing just this.

Personal data bought and sold includes everything from your web-browsing habits and interests to your location history. The least-worst case is that your personal data is purchased by companies wanting to target you with ads. In the worst case, hackers gain access to that data, where it is made available to scammers and identity thieves.

You can fight back using what’s known as “takedown requests.” By law, data brokers have to remove your data if you tell them to. However, this is much easier said than done.

First, you would have to contact literally hundreds of different companies. Second, many of those companies deliberately make takedown links hard to find, then force you to jump through all sorts of hoops in order to issue the requests. Some of them even break the law by not providing the links in the first place.

But even if you succeed, the results won’t last for long. Data brokers are constantly buying new data and adding it to your profile. It’s a constant game of whack-a-mole.

That’s where Incogni comes in. Not only do they do all of the hard work for you across literally hundreds of data brokers, genealogy websites, and social media, but they monitor to ensure that it has been done, scan for the later addition of new data, and issue new takedown requests for that.

Unlike other services, Incogni helps remove your sensitive information from all broker types, including those tricky People Search Sites that are often missed.

With the company’s Unlimited plan, you can even send links you’ve discovered yourself and Incogni will take care of it for you.
